settings.heading: The two objections come before the miles do.
settings.lede: Runners ask about weight and bulk before anything else, and they are right to. Here is the honest version of that trade, and what the sock is actually for.
settings.image_alt: Running & Trail in HydroSox waterproof socks

settings.heading: Wet feet are a race problem, not a comfort problem.
settings.lede: On a long winter run the cost of soaked feet is not that they feel unpleasant. It is that wet skin blisters, and a blister at eight miles decides the rest of the run.

settings.title: Softened skin gives up early
settings.body: Wet skin under repeated rub is the blister mechanism. Dry skin takes considerably more of it before it breaks down.

settings.title: Trail shoes are built to drain
settings.body: A mesh upper is designed to let water out, which necessarily means letting it in. That is the right design for the shoe. It still leaves the foot wet.

settings.title: Cold arrives with the wet
settings.body: A soaked foot at winter temperatures gets cold quickly and stays cold, however hard the rest of you is working.

settings.heading: What it is, without the marketing.
settings.head_note: It is a three-layer sock with a membrane in it, so it is thicker than a racing sock. It is not a compression sock and it is not a lightweight. Knowing that is what lets you decide correctly.

settings.title: The membrane is the point
settings.body: A licensed Porelle® waterproof-breathable laminate between two knits. Water stops at the sock; vapour still moves outward.

settings.title: Thicker than a race sock — that is the trade
settings.body: Three bonded layers are not as thin as a single-layer technical sock. On wet winter miles that trade is usually worth taking. In a dry summer 10k it is not.

settings.title: Crew height, above the shoe
settings.body: The cuff clears a trail shoe collar, which is also where most of the spray and grit arrives.

settings.heading: The same pair, in the conditions this page is about.
settings.head_note: Product imagery rather than a documentary shoot, so read it for what the sock is and where it goes — not as evidence. The checkable claim is the membrane.

settings.title: Try them on a training run first
settings.body: Never on race day. Any change in sock thickness changes how a shoe fits, and a race is the wrong place to find that out.

settings.title: Wet-weather kit, not everyday kit
settings.body: Plenty of runners keep a pair for winter and wet races and run in their usual socks the rest of the year. That is a reasonable way to use them.

settings.title: Cool wash, no conditioner or dryer
settings.body: Standard care for anything with a membrane in it.

settings.heading: The honest limit.
settings.body: Breathable does not mean dry inside. Run hard enough and you will sweat faster than any membrane can move vapour — so on a hard effort your feet will be damp from the inside, at body temperature, rather than cold from a puddle. That is a real difference. It is also not the same as dry.
settings.footnote: Every limit we know about is published, not only this one. Read the rest.
